sections.html:
Jeffersonville, seat of Clark County, faces Louisville, Kentucky across the Ohio River, with Interstate 65 running through town. The population rose from 27,362 in 2000 to 49,447 in 2020. Median owner-occupied value is $216,800, and 72.0% of housing units are lived in by owners.

Averages hide a lot. A house in the old river neighborhoods and one in a newer annexed area such as Oak Park can be worlds apart. Buyers weigh the commute across the river, and they know areas by names like Port Fulton, Warder Park and Big Four Station, so use whichever name a buyer will recognize.

Because of the Ohio River, flooding is the main property question in Jeffersonville. In 1937 about 90% of the city went under water, and the city still regulates building in the floodplain. Jeffersonville takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program. Flood maps sit at the Building Commissioner's office, 500 Quartermaster Court, phone 812-285-6412.

  • Fill, excavation, fences and other development in the 100-year floodplain may need a city permit.
  • Repairs or improvements costing over 50% of a building's market value, land excluded, pull the entire building under current floodplain standards.
  • Elevation Certificates for buildings in the Special Flood Hazard Area are on file with the city and can lower insurance rates.
  • A federally backed mortgage on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area requires flood insurance.

NFIP coverage tops out at $250,000 for a single-family home. The city's Level 8 Community Rating System rating earns a 10% discount on policies in a Special Flood Hazard Area.

sections.h2: How floodplain status changes a sale
sections.html:
If your house lies in a Special Flood Hazard Area, a buyer with a bank loan must buy flood insurance. That can lower what the buyer offers or slow the closing.

Not sure which zone you are in? Use the city's interactive map, or ask the Building Commissioner to look up an elevation certificate. If a flood determination looks wrong to you, FEMA accepts a Letter of Determination Review request within 45 days.

Pull together these papers before listing:

  • The declarations page of your flood policy, if you carry one.
  • An elevation certificate, if one exists.
  • Records of repairs and permits.
  • Notes on any time water got in.

The 50% rule deserves a close look before you spend anything. When improvements or repairs on a floodplain building add up to more than half of its market value, excluding land, the whole building has to meet current floodplain standards. A seller who plans a big renovation before listing could trigger it by accident.

Start with a list of what a buyer's inspector would flag, then get rough estimates. Compare the cost and the weeks of work with the price a buyer would pay for the house as it stands. If the work comes close to the 50% line, or you cannot front the money, selling as-is avoids the question completely. Ask the Building Commissioner whether a permit applies before any fill, excavation or fence work.

Clark County records Jeffersonville deeds at the Recorder's Office, 300 Corporate Drive, Room 102, phone 812-285-6235. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., though documents must arrive by 4:00 p.m. to be recorded that day.

The route runs through three rooms: the Assessor in Room 104 reviews the deed, the Auditor in Room 106 transfers it, and fees are paid at both offices.

Paperwork on the deed includes a notary acknowledgment, a prepared-by statement, an affirmation that Social Security numbers are redacted, the legal description and the buyer's address. Indiana also asks for a sales disclosure form. A title company usually handles the lot.

Jeffersonville owners pay property tax in a spring and a fall installment, May 10 and November 10. When a sale closes near one of those dates, the closing agent splits the installment between you and the buyer, and any tax still owed comes out of your proceeds. Phone the county for your current balance before you accept an offer.

Greater Clark County Schools serves the city, so buyers with children ask which elementary and middle school a street feeds. Interstate 65 runs straight to Louisville, and the Big Four Bridge offers a walking route over the river.

Typical Jeffersonville sellers own an older river-neighborhood house, have a floodplain question or have a tenant living there.

  • Flood insurance cost and what lenders require.
  • Repairs nearing the 50% limit in the floodplain.
  • Inherited houses on older streets.
  • A move over the river or out of the area.

Get every term in writing, whichever way you go. Settle who covers title work and recording, whether the buyer will inspect, and the closing date. If the house is in a floodplain, say so early, because flood insurance quotes take time and some lenders want one before closing.

sections.h2: Steps from first call to closing
sections.html:
1. Send us the address and tell us about the house, any tenants and any flood history.
  2. We look at the property and make an offer.
  3. If you accept, a title company opens the file and searches the deed for liens and unpaid taxes.
  4. You sign the deed paperwork and the sales disclosure form.
  5. The deed goes through the Assessor, the Auditor and the Recorder, and you collect your proceeds.

Most delays come from the title search or a missing document, such as a notary acknowledgment or a legal description. Raise anything you suspect on the first call.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works here
sections.html:
We buy Jeffersonville houses as-is, including houses with flood damage. You describe the property, we make an offer, and if you accept, a title company searches the deed and sets the closing date. A cash buyer does not depend on a lender's flood insurance requirement, so that issue does not hold up the closing. Disclose what you know about past water entry and compare written offers.

Bring your tax bill, any flood insurance page, elevation certificate and repair records to the first call. A short list of what you know about the house, written down before you talk to any buyer, makes every conversation faster.

An inherited house in an older river neighborhood often needs probate before a deed can be prepared, and it may need a clean-out as well. Heirs who live across the river or farther away end up paying utilities, insurance and tax on a house nobody lives in. Gather the estate papers, the tax bill and the keys, then ask the title company what the deed needs before closing. An as-is sale ends the monthly costs and spares repeat trips.

faqs.q: Is Jeffersonville in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of it are. The city participates in the National Flood Insurance Program and publishes flood maps and an interactive map. Check your parcel with the Building Commissioner at 812-285-6412.

faqs.q: Do I need flood insurance to sell my Jeffersonville house?
faqs.a: You do not need it to sell, but a buyer with a federally backed mortgage on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area must carry it. Expect questions about it.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Jeffersonville?
faqs.a: At the Clark County Recorder's Office, 300 Corporate Drive, Room 102. The deed is first reviewed by the Assessor and transferred by the Auditor.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Clark County?
faqs.a: The recorder charges $25.00 for deeds and other instruments, and fees are also paid at the Auditor's office.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Jeffersonville house that has flood damage?
faqs.a: Yes. Disclose what you know and compare written offers. Cash buyers can purchase a house with damage as is.
